Watershed: Third Creek, Incline Creek, Wood Creek, Griff Creek, Second Creek, Tahoe Vista, First Creek, Burnt Cedar Creek, Mill Creek, East Stateline Point, Carnelian Canyon, Kings Beach, Ward Creek, Watson, Tunnel Creek, Carnelian Bay Creek, Bonpland, Cedar Flats, Barton Creek, Dollar Creek, Burton Creek, Sand Harbor, Lake Forest Creek, Marlette Creek, Tahoe State Park, Truckee River, Secret Harbor Creek, Bliss Creek, Deadman Point, Slaughter House, Blackwood Creek, Glenbrook Creek, Eagle Rock, North Logan House Creek, Madden Creek, Homewood Creek, Quail Lake Creek, Mckinney Creek, Logan House Creek, General Creek, Cave Rock, Lincoln Creek, Meeks Creek, North Zephyr Creek, Skyland, Zephyr Creek, Sierra Creek, Mcfaul Creek, Lonely Gulch Creek, Paradise Flat, South Zephyr Creek, Burke Creek, Rubicon Creek, Bliss State Park, Edgewood Creek, Bijou Park, Eagle Creek, Cascade Creek, Bijou Creek, Tallac Creek, Upper Truckee River, Trout Creek, Camp Richardson, Taylor Creek, Lake Tahoe Waterbody
ProjectDescription: Keep Tahoe Blue Schools is the Keep Tahoe Blue’s youth education program to provide environmental science and stewardship experiences for Lake Tahoe area students. Keep Tahoe Blue connects Tahoe’s students with their environment and aims to foster a lifelong sense of appreciation and responsibility for Lake Tahoe through place-based education. Keep Tahoe Blue Schools partners with local organizations and agencies, teaches lessons in classrooms and on field trips, and includes an innovative multidisciplinary program, Curriculum for Lake Education, Awareness, and Responsibility (CLEAR), based on Common Core Standards to provide long-term learning opportunities.

ProjectName: High Efficiency Street Sweeper Purchase
Watershed: Mckinney Creek, General Creek, Meeks Creek, Sierra Creek, Lonely Gulch Creek, Paradise Flat, Rubicon Creek, Bliss State Park, Edgewood Creek, Bijou Park, Eagle Creek, Cascade Creek, Bijou Creek, Tallac Creek, Upper Truckee River, Trout Creek, Camp Richardson, Taylor Creek, Lake Tahoe Waterbody
ProjectDescription: This project supports operations and maintenance of capital projects by upgrading equipment to support current air quality standards through equipment upgrades. This project purchased a Tymco 500X and will improve the clarity of Lake Tahoe by reducing the detrimental water quality impacts from El Dorado County roadways. The purchase and use of high efficiency sweepers has been proven to reduce fine sediment particles and nutrient loading from urban roadways and reduce the amount of fine sediment particles that become airborne.

ProjectName: South Upper Truckee Water Quality Project
ProjectDescription: The South Upper Truckee Water Quality Project (Project) encompasses Tahoe Paradise Unit 60, River Park Estates Units 1 & 2, and South Gate Subdivisions.  This includes the neighborhoods off of South Upper Truckee Road, bordered by US 50 to the north, the Upper Truckee River to the south and east, and USFS owned parcels to the west.  The primary goal of the Project is to improve the clarity of Lake Tahoe by reducing detrimental water quality impacts that are a result of the development of the subdivisions, including the reduction of the transport of fine sediment from the Project area to the Upper Truckee River by construction of appropriate water quality BMPs.

ProjectName: Kings Beach Pier Reconstruction
LeadImplementerName: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ProjectDescription: The project revises the 1980 General Plan for Kings Beach State Recreation Area (KBSRA), expands the KBSRA boundary to include the 1.36-acre Kings Beach Plaza (Plaza), and considers potential land ownership transfer of the Plaza to State Parks.  The General Plan revision would provide a comprehensive framework for projects within, and management of, KBSRA over the next 20 years.  The project also includes three locational alternatives for rebuilding the Kings Beach pier to a standard that increases its functionality for boating.  The preferred pier location is to the east end of KBSRA.

ProjectName: Zephyr Cove Elementary School Science Center
ProjectDescription: An indoor/outdoor place-based science classroom located at Zephyr Cove Elementary School. This classroom will be open to all schools in the Region as a center for students to learn about the environment and Lake Tahoe while doing science and having fun. Designed for K-6 students with curriculum based on the program areas of the Environmental Improvement Program.

ProjectName: Edgewood Lodge and Golf Course Improvement
ProjectDescription: The project is located at the bottom of the Edgewood Creek watershed which drains an area of approximately 6.6 square miles. Mixed land uses within the watershed interrupted the natural hydrologic processes, and the resulting influx of nutrients and sediment degraded the quality of the watershed. This project included construction of a new 194-unit lodge complex and a series of environmental improvements including enhanced BMPs for the lodge complex, water quality improvements to the pond system, Edgewood Creek improvements, Friday’s Station dam rehabilitation, and undergrounding of existing overhead utility lines.

ProjectName: Iroquois Pond, Mountain View Well and Tata Wells and Tank SEZ Restoration
ProjectDescription: This project is the planning, design and environmental requirements necessary to implement the Stream Environmental Zone restoration of three key STPUD sites:  Iroquois Pond, Mountain View Well and Tata Wells and Tank.  The goal of this project is to implement the best management practices and SEZ restoration plans developed for each site in order to benefit the water quality of Lake Tahoe by reducing erosion, sediment flow and surface water runoff originating from these three sites.  The three sites are listed together as one project for planning purposes and because of their similarities.

ProjectName: Stream Environment Zone Utility Crossing Condition Assessment
Watershed: Bijou Park, Bijou Creek, Upper Truckee River, Trout Creek, Camp Richardson, Lake Tahoe Waterbody
ProjectDescription: STPUD has approximately 149 sites in which utility infrastructure (water and sewer lines) are crossing a stream environment zone, under or in the streambed.  This project is a condition assessment of each of these 149 sites in order to assess the condition of the current infrastructure and the risk to the SEZ.  The assessment would prioritize the sites through a risk assessment and give a generalized "toolbox" approach to stabilizing the infrastructure, to include stream restoration as necessary.

ProjectName: Upper Truckee River Utility Crossing
ProjectDescription: STPUD has a waterline located in Tahoe Paradise Park near Lake Baron that crosses the Upper Truckee River.  The utility line is at critical risk for failure due to stream erosion/morphology issues. This project is the design and implementation of improvements to the existing waterline by installing a redundant waterline on the Pedestrian/Bike Bridge that is to be constructed by the County. This waterline is the main source of water supply to over 3,000 homes in Tahoe Paradise.

ProjectName: Tahoe Keys Lagoon Aquatic Weeds Control Methods Test Implementation
ProjectDescription: The Control Methods Test was approved by TRPA and Lahontan in January 2022, and implementation of the full test- ultraviolet light, aquatic herbicides and other non-herbicidal methods- began in May of 2022. In addition to the test treatment methods, extensive monitoring is being conducted to follow herbicide degradation, water quality conditions, and efficacy of treatment methods.

ProjectName: Tahoe Keys Lagoons Aquatic Weeds Control Methods Test Planning
ProjectDescription: The Tahoe Keys Lagoons are a series of waterways directly connected to Lake Tahoe that are almost entirely infested with invasive aquatic weeds. At over 170 acres, it is the largest aquatic weed infestation in the lake. The Tahoe Keys Lagoons Aquatic Weed Control Methods Test is collaboratively developed project that seeks to test multiple methods of weed control to gain information on what combination of methods will have the best chance of treating the entirety of the Tahoe Keys Lagoons infestation. The environmental analysis and test project was approved by boards from TRPA and Lahontan in January 2022, with implementation slated for the Spring of 2022. Implementation project 01.03.01.000

ProjectName: Upper Haines Canyon - Kingsbury 1000
ProjectDescription: The Upper Haines Canyon Fuels Reduction Project is a 72 acre fuels reduction project located in Haines Canyon Nevada.  Haines Canyon is a steep v-shaped canyon formed by Daggett Creek.  The canyon runs from 4700 feet in elevation where it crosses Foothill Road and extends up to the summit of Kingbury Grade at an elevation of 7350 feet.  The canyon extends from the Lake Tahoe Basin down to Carson Valley.  As such, the valley is subject to diurnal winds typical of mountain canyons.  The units within the project are designed to create survivable space around homes within the canyon and to further treat fuels located within Upper Haines Canyon.

ProjectName: Burton Creek Forest Restoration and Prescribed Fire
LeadImplementerName: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ProjectDescription: Forest thinning with hand crews and prescribed fire will be implemented to reduce hazardous fuels and enhance residual tree species health. This project is designed to reduce tree densities in order to modify fire behavior to reduce the potential for a catastrophic, stand replacement fire. Forest thinning with hand crews will prepare burn plots for treatment with understory prescribed fire.  Implement understory prescribed fire in four burn plots.

ProjectName: Forestry - Barbara Lodi hand crew
ProjectDescription: The Barbara Lodi forestry project involves cutting of trees that were marked under the guidance of a RPF for forest health and fuel reduction efforts. The project was implemented by hand crews cutting designated trees and brush.  The project is split into two phases, the first being the cutting of designated trees and brush and the second being the burning of the piles. The project is located in the south shore,  in the vicinity of Barbara and Lodi Streets, of Lake Tahoe and is 7 acres in size.

ProjectName: Forestry - SNPLMA 14 Fairway
ProjectDescription: 6 acres of pile and burn.

ProjectName: Forestry - SNPLMA 14 Sunset
ProjectDescription: Fuel hazard reduction by hand crew thinning conifers and piling for burning - 6 acres

ProjectName: Forestry - Sunset South
ProjectDescription: The Sunset South forestry project involves cutting of trees that were marked under the guidance of a RPF for forest health and fuel reduction efforts. The project was implemented by hand crews cutting designated trees and brush.  The project is split into two phases, the first being the cutting of designated trees and brush and the second being the burning of the piles. The project is located in the south shore, at the southeast end of the Conservancy's Sunset Stables property,  of Lake Tahoe and is 40 acres in size.

ProjectName: Forestry - Mongomery Estates
ProjectDescription: 34 acres of reducing conifer and other forest fuels on Tahoe Conservancy-owned urban lots using hand crew thinning and chipping

ProjectName: Crystal Shores Aquatic Invasive Plant Control
ProjectDescription: The aquatic plant removal work implemented at Crystal Shores West, Crystal Shores East, and Crystal Shores Villas was part of a multi-year lake-wide strategy to remove aquatic invasive plants from the nearshore of Lake Tahoe Basin. From 2014-2016, contracted divers used lake-bottom barriers, diver-assisted suction removal, and hand-pulling to remove 100% of the Eurasian watermilfoil in all three marinas. From 2017-2019, contracted divers surveyed all three marinas several times during the growing season and hand-pulled any plants detected (2 total).

ProjectName: Fleur du Lac Aquatic Invasive Plant Control
ProjectDescription: Aquatic plant removal at Fleur du Lac Marina and the outer harbor is part of a multi-year lake-wide strategy to remove aquatic invasive plants from the nearshore of Lake Tahoe Basin. Bottom barriers, diver-assisted suction removal, and hand-pulling were used from 2016-2018 to reduce the Eurasian watermilfoil infestation to 0% cover. From 2018-2020, divers conducted surveillance monitoring to ensure there is not a re-occurence of this infestation. Surveillance monitoring was not conducted in 2021, but is expected to be re-initiated in 2021 and will continue to occur at this site annually (funding-dependent).

ProjectName: Lakeside Marina Aquatic Invasive Plant Control
ProjectDescription: The Eurasian watermilfoil and curlyleaf pondweed infestation covers approximately 1 acre inside and immediately adjacent to the marina. Ultraviolet light, benthic barriers, diver-assisted suction removal, and hand-pulling are being used to control these plant species. This project is being implemented in coordination with EIP Project Number 01.03.01.0030, Lakeside Beach & Marina Aquatic Invasive Plant Control UV Light Pilot II.

ProjectName: Lakeside Beach Aquatic Invasive Plant Control
ProjectDescription: The Eurasian watermilfoil and curly-leaf pondweed infestation at Lakeside Beach (swim area) is approximately 1 acre. These species have been removed using benthic barriers, diver-assisted suction removal, and hand-pulling. This project is being implemented in coordination with EIP Project Number 01.03.01.0030, Lakeside Beach & Marina Aquatic Invasive Plant Control UV Light Pilot II.

ProjectName: Meeks Bay Aquatic Invasive Species Plant Control and Monitoring
LeadImplementerName: U.S. Forest Service - Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit
ProjectDescription: In 2015, the AIS Implementation Plan (Plan) and associated Action list prioritized projects for AIS control. Meeks Bay Marina is prioritized in the Plan because Eurasian watermilfoil occupy this habitat in the Marina. This project focuses on removal of the Eurasian watermilfoil infestation and associated monitoring. A contract was awarded in 2019 to initiate removal efforts of approximately three acres of invasive weeds in the footprint of the marina and upstream to the SR89 bridge. Treatment occurred 2019 through 2022. The treatment area is now in control monitoring to ensure it remains weed free. The project is expected to move to surveillance monitoring after 2025.

ProjectName: Ski Run Channel Aquatic Invasive Plant Control
ProjectDescription: The Eurasian watermilfoil and curly-leaf pondweed infestation is approximately 3.5 acres. The size and complexity of this infestation requires an integrated approach that includes treatment of the infestation in the adjacent Ski Run Marina.

ProjectName: Ski Run Marina Aquatic Invasive Plant Control
ProjectDescription: The infestation at Ski Run Marina will now be addressed through a new project that addresses multiple locations along the south shore as monitoring has revealed there is no distinct beginning or end of a project area: South Shore Offshore Aquatic Invasive Plant Planning and Control- 01.03.01.0051i

ProjectName: Truckee River Aquatic Invasive Plant Control
ProjectDescription: This project area is located immediately downstream from the dam located in Tahoe City. In 2019, it was determined that the infestation extended for ~3 miles and it was estimated that 15-20% of this area is infested with Eurasian watermilfoil. Techniques for removal are determined by water level, flow rates, and recreational use, and include bottom barriers, diver-assisted suction removal, and hand pulling. Because of the large extent of this infestation and lack of a more recent survey of the infestation, renewed planning to engage appropriate partners, and an effort to solicit funding is needed.

ProjectName: D.L Bliss Campground Hazardous Fuel Reduction
LeadImplementerName: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ProjectDescription: Forest thinning and fuel reduction took place to reduce hazardous fuels on 33 acres at D.L. Bliss State Park to protect forest resources, watershed resources, sensitive wildlife habitat, visitor safety and outdoor recreation while improving the resiliency of the forest.

ProjectName: D.L Bliss SNPLMA Round 15 Hazardous Fuel Reduction
LeadImplementerName: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ProjectDescription: Forest thinning with hand crews and prescribed fire will be implemented to reduce hazardous fuels and enhance residual tree species health. This project is designed to reduce tree densities in order to modify fire behavior to reduce the potential for a catastrophic, stand replacement fire. Forest thinning with hand crews will reduce ladder fuels, overcrowded/diseased trees and enhance forest health. Thinned trees and dead and downed woody debris will be piled throughout the spring, summer and fall months and burned in the fall/winter.

ProjectName: D.L. Bliss Gateway Hazardous Fuel Reduction
LeadImplementerName: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ProjectDescription: Forest thinning with hand crews and prescribed fire will be implemented to reduce hazardous fuels and enhance residual tree species health. This project is designed to reduce tree densities in order to modify fire behavior to reduce the potential for a catastrophic, stand replacement fire. Forest thinning with hand crews will reduce ladder fuels, overcrowded/diseased trees and enhance forest health. Thinned trees and dead and downed woody debris will be piled throughout the spring, summer and fall months and burned in the fall/winter.

ProjectName: Sugar Pine SNPLMA Round 14 Hazardous Fuel Reduction
LeadImplementerName: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ProjectDescription: This project included forest thinning with hand crews and prescribed fire to reduce hazardous fuels and enhance residual tree species health.  This project was designed to reduce tree densities in order to modify fire behavior to reduce the potential for a catastrophic, stand replacement fire. Forest thinning by hand crews reduced ladder fuels, overcrowded/diseased trees and enhance forest health. Thinned trees and dead and downed woody debris were piled throughout the spring, summer and fall months and burned in the fall/winter.

ProjectName: Westshore Wildland Urban Interface (WUI) Hazardous Fuels Reduction and Forest Health Project
LeadImplementerName: U.S. Forest Service - Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit
ProjectDescription: The West Shore WUI Project proposes vegetation and fuels treatments to reduce stand densities to improve forest health, reduce fire hazards from existing fuels, and modify fire behavior to provide defensible space for adjoining developed private lands. Treatment options include ground based mechanical treatments wherever slope and road access allow, and hand treatments where steeper and/or rocky slopes prohibit mechanical equipment operations. The proposed action includes 110 treatment units, and approximately 100 urban lots, totaling approximately 4,875 acres.

ProjectName: High Meadows Phase II- east and middle meadow
LeadImplementerName: U.S. Forest Service - Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit
ProjectDescription: This project is implementing a phase of meadow/riparian area restoration work identified within and around the 185-acre High Meadows Complex and thinning of the forest surrounding the meadow.  This project would implement restoration actions to enhance 120 acres of meadow/riparian habitat through removal of lodgepole pine encroachment in and around the meadow, and an additional 1.5 miles of stream/floodplain restoration. Stream restoration would include replacing stream flow into constructed and historic channels where they are currently flowing in ditches, filling of existing ditches, placing large wood in the channel, and constructing smaller in-channel structures.

ProjectName: Kings Beach Western Approach
ProjectDescription: Multi-benefit project improving the mobility, walkability, water quality improvements and sustainability at the SR 267/SR 28 intersection. The existing signalized intersection at State Route (SR) 267 and SR 28 in Kings Beach limits vehicular flow during higher traffic volume periods. The project would convert the intersection to a roundabout considered to be an improvement in mobility, safety and efficiency, and LOS. Includes enhanced public transit access, sidewalks, bike lanes (Class II ) connection.  Project components will include acquisition of private ROW to meet goals and objectives.

This is Project Number TR-08 in the 2015 Tahoe Basin ITS Strategic Plan.

ProjectName: TTD Transit Technology and Amenities
ProjectDescription: Electronic Log Book, Electronic Daily Vehicle Inspection verification, additional electic vehicle charging infrastructure, information technology enhancements such as cable and fiber access. Bus Stops, Real-Time Arrival Screens, Wifi hotpoints, Shelters, ADA improvements, Benches, and transit optimization measures. Implementation of transit technology and amenities will reduce reliance on the private automobile, reduce airborne and particulate emissions, and improve air and water quality.

ProjectName: Nevada Stateline to Stateline Corridor Improvements - Glenbrook Entrance to Round Hill Pines Beach
ProjectDescription:
This project includes segments D, E, and F, identified in the Nevada Stateline-to-Stateline Bikeway Project Feasibility Study Report, completed in June 2011.  
Segment D: Glenbrook Entrance to Cave Rock Drive, estimated cost: $15M
Segment E: Cave Rock Drive to Zephyr Cove, estimated cost: $11M
Segment F: Zephyr Cove to Round Hill Pines Beach Entrance: $6M

ProjectName: Lake Tahoe Boulevard Class 1 Bicycle Trail (Viking Way to South Wye)
ProjectDescription:
Design and construct Class 1 bike trail, ADA compliant ramps, and pathway lighting along the 0.6 mile section of Lake Tahoe Blvd. from the Intersection of Viking Way (D-Street) to the intersection of State Hwy 89 and US Highway 50 (South Wye).
Note: Project name was updated from "Viking Way to Lake Tahoe Blvd. Class 1 Bike Trail" on 11/23/16 for consistency with the name CSLT used to apply for CMAQ funds.

ProjectName: Upper Cold Creek Watershed Restoration
Jurisdiction: City of South Lake Tahoe, Douglas County, NV, El Dorado County, CA
ProjectDescription: Project involves work on the Upper Cold Creek stream banks and restoration of previous channel disturbances to stabilize the streambanks, restore SEZ areas and improve the existing non-motorized bicycle and footpaths along this segment of Cold Creek.

ProjectName: Trout and Cold Creek Watershed Assessment and Restoration
Jurisdiction: City of South Lake Tahoe, Douglas County, NV, El Dorado County, CA
ProjectDescription: The project is starting with a watershed assessment of the Trout Creek and Cold Creek drainages. The goal of the project is to restore and enhance Stream Environment Zone (SEZ) ecosystem function within the watershed. The work includes a general assessment of the watersheds to identify key processes or factors that may influence the planning and design of restoration opportunities. The Conservancy will identify restoration opportunities, including conifer removal, focusing on publicly owned SEZs in the lower Trout Creek and Cold Creek watersheds, between Highway 50 and Pioneer Trail, and up Cold Creek to Powerline Trail, over approximately 280 acres.

ProjectName: Street Sweeper Purchase
ProjectDescription: Purchase two (2) new Elgin Eagle PM-10 Sweepers to replace two (2)  existing Tymco Sweepers that were purchased in 2008 and have exceeded Lifespan.  The City of South Lake Tahoe utilizes three (3) street sweepers to remove sediment and debris from approx 259 lane miles of City roads and trails.   The City purchased two Tymco PM-10 sweepers in 2008 through a combination of TRPA AQ & WQ Mitigation funds and City General Funds.   The Tymco's have reached the end of usable life span (Typically 5-7 years for most agencies).  The wear on internal operating parts has become severe and repair costs in both parts and labor dictate replacement is warranted.

ProjectName: Sander Truck upgrade to reduce emissions and abrasives
Watershed: Bijou Park, Bijou Creek, Upper Truckee River, Trout Creek, Camp Richardson, Lake Tahoe Waterbody
ProjectDescription: Replace existing sander/spreader truck with new truck and Epoke abrasives distribution system.  The Epoke system provides control over dispersion of all sanding materials — dry, pre-wet or liquid.  Not only preserving the natural environment, but also reducing wasted material and excessive damage to infrastructure (bridges, culverts, etc.).  Epoke provides technology to greater control the amount of material used, type of distribution, and area of coverage, using significantly less material while providing a more uniform coverage with just one pass.  Utilization of less material results in less materials become airborne, dispersed into storm drains and ultimately reduces recovery time

ProjectName: Incline Village Bike Park
ProjectDescription: IVGID in partnership with the Incline Tahoe Foundation (ITF) and the Incline Bike Park (IBP) have come together in hopes of building a bike park in Incline Village, NV.  This would build a community park for all age groups and abilities to enjoy.  The Bike Park would be centrally located in town to allow users to ride their bikes to the park, instead of driving.  As seen at other similar venues in the Tahoe Basin, bike parks are a family centered event that get folks out of their cars and can have a lasting impact on human health as well as improve air quality.  This recreational project will have a lasting impact on the community with a low carbon footprint and a high return on investment.

ProjectName: Recreation and Swim Center Renovation/Replacement
ProjectDescription: Replacement of existing City Recreation and Swim Center with new energy efficient and multi use facility.

ProjectName: Truckee River Dam Aquatic Invasive Plant Control
ProjectDescription: The aquatic plant removal work being implemented above Lake Tahoe Dam is part of a multi-year lake-wide strategy to remove Eurasian watermilfoil from the nearshore of Lake Tahoe. Divers primarily use hand-pulling at this site to remove Eurasian watermilfoil that periodically appears rooted here. In 2022, surveillance maintenance of this site is being transferred to EIP Project Number 01.03.01.0037 Lake-wide Surveillance and Site Assessments. The surveillance survey area is approximately 1.6 acres.

ProjectName: Emerald Bay Aquatic Invasive Species Asian Clam Control
ProjectDescription: A relatively sparse population of Asian clams were discovered near the mouth of Emerald Bay in 2009. Initial surveys estimated this infestation at approximately 3.5 acres in size just inside and on the south side of the mouth of Emerald Bay, in water depths of six (6) to thirty (30) feet. Surveys in 2011 showed the infestation had spread to approximately 5.5 acres (2011 U.C. Davis Survey Results), an increase in infestation size of over forty percent (40%) in only two (2) years. An expansion of the Emerald Bay infestation similar to that seen in South Lake Tahoe would result in considerable ecological and recreation impacts.

ProjectName: Elk Point Marina Aquatic Invasive Plant Control
ProjectDescription: Bottom barriers, diver-assisted suction removal and hand-pulling were used to control plants in the marina. In addition, the League to Save Lake Tahoe provided homeowners with Eyes on the Lake training to learn how to identify and report aquatic invasive plants. Effectively controlling plant fragments from entering the marina from Lake Tahoe continues to be a challenge. A bubble curtain was installed in 2021 at the mouth of the marina to reduce invasive aquatic plant fragments from re-infesting the area and to protect the investment. In 2025, diver-assisted suction removal was conducted, and diver surveys and plant removal will continue in 2026 and 2027.

ProjectName: Multi-Modal Recreational Use Upgrades on Roads

This project is ITS Plan MT-02 and is jointly led by Caltrans and NDOT.

ProjectName: Upper Griff Creek Bridge Replacement
ProjectDescription:
This project will replace a log bridge spanning Griff Creek that collapsed in 2013. Since its collapse, the public has been traversing through the creek to gain recreational access. This use has degraded the sensitive stream environment. 

The USDA Forest Service, Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit applied for and was awarded a California State Parks OHMVR Commission grant in August 2020 for $243,618 to replace the bridge. 

Conservancy staff received authorization from their Board in June 2021 to provide up to $150,000 in Habitat Conservation Fund (HCF) funding to serve as a match to the LTBMU grant. 

Anticipated construction of the new bridge will begin August 2026.

This program is funded by the Airport Enterprise Fund operations budget and through grants from the Federal Aviation Administration and the State of California.  These include forest fuel reduction and fire resilience in areas surrounding the airport, and habitat modification to reduce the likelihood of wildlife/aircraft collisions.  All efforts are supported for regulatory compliance through a contract Registered Professional Forester and a contract Wildlife Biologist.  Project completed on November 19, 2021.

ProjectName: Preston Field Water Quality Improvement Project - Phase I
ProjectDescription: This is a water quality improvement project located in Incline Village. The area is highly connected to Lake Tahoe and has a relatively large baseline FSP load. The project proposes to install stormwater treatment BMPs and shoulder stabilization within the existing Washoe County right-of-way and undeveloped public parcels, providing treatment for urban stormwater runoff to meet the Lake Tahoe TMDL.

ProjectName: Lower Wood Creek Water Quality Improvement Project - Phase 1
ProjectDescription:
This water quality improvement project in a priority treatment area in Incline Village reduces the amount of fine sediment washing into the lake and help Washoe County meet its milestone of the Lake Tahoe TMDL and improve lake clarity. 

Tasks include installation of stormwater treatment BMPs, shoulder stabilization, and culvert improvements. Benefits include improved stormwater quality release to Wood Creek & Lake Tahoe, increased protection and stream function for Wood Creek riparian and SEZ and greater TRPA Stormwater Program collaboration for BMP compliance. The project (Phase 1 & 2) is expected to earn Washoe County 30-40 credits in the Lake Clarity Crediting Program.

ProjectName: Upper Third & Rosewood Creeks Water Quality Improvement Project - Phase I
ProjectDescription: This water quality improvement project is located in Incline Village. The area is highly connected to Lake Tahoe and is a priority treatment area due to a relatively large baseline FSP load. The project proposes to install stormwater treatment BMPs and shoulder stabilization within the existing Washoe County right-of-way and undeveloped public parcels, providing treatment for urban stormwater runoff to meet the Lake Tahoe TMDL. This project is on the 5-year list. Washoe County secured planning and design funding and has hired a consultant. The first TAC was held in December 2025. the Project will be implemented in two Phases.

ProjectName: Meeks Meadow Restoration

Phase 3: Implementation and construct

ProjectDescription: The Lake Tahoe Public Access Strategic Investment Plan (Plan) will serve as a planning resource for future public access, where lawful and feasible, to and along Lake Tahoe’s shoreline. Ultimately, the Plan will help further attainment of the Tahoe Region’s Recreation Environmental Threshold and other regional planning objectives by providing information to direct public access funding investment over the next 5-10 years to both optimize use of existing facilities and to identify opportunities for additional public access, while considering the compatibility of public access in balance with environmental and public constraints. The 2017 effort includes CA inventory and documentation only.

ProjectName: Rehabilitate Meyers Creek - Lake Valley State Rec Area Reach
LeadImplementerName: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ProjectDescription: Restore Meyers Creek (a tributary/infeeder stream) in vicinity of Hole 18 of the Lake Tahoe Golf Course in Lake Valley State Recreation Area.  The golf course was constructed in late 1950's (prior to current standards for erosion and water runoff control) and stream was channelized into a ditch.  Project includes construction of a more sinuous channel and revegetation to improve value as wildlife habitat.  This project is associated with proposed Upper Truckee River Restoration at Lake Tahoe Golf Course.

ProjectName: 2016 NDF-SFA Fuels Reduction and Community Education and Outreach - Forest Thinning Component
LeadImplementerName: North Lake Tahoe Fire Protection District
ProjectDescription: This project will reduce hazardous fuels and restore forest health on 20.5 acres of privately owned property within the Wildland Urban Interface of Incline Village, NV.   There are 27 homes within and adjacent to the project area and 670 more homes within one-quarter mile. Two of the parcels serve to connect current and planned fuels reduction projects on federally owned land managed by the USFS.  Crews will hand thin hazardous fuels to reduce potential fire behavior to a level that permits direct attack by first responders. Cut material will be piled and burned, or left on site in preparation for understory burning.

ProjectName: Highway 50 Fuels Reduction Project
ProjectDescription: This project reduced the risk of catastrophic fire and resulting damage to communities by reducing wildland fuels within the Wildland Urban Interface (WUI). The project areas were all located within the Defense Zone of the Tahoe Douglas Fire Protection District WUI and are all immediately adjacent to U.S. Forest Service Lands that have been treated.  The project was composed of 138 acres over 6 units.  The largest unit was a 100 acre property located between the communities of Round Hill and Zephyr Heights.  The other units average 7 acres and was located within communities along Highway 50 from Stateline to near Glenbrook.

ProjectName: SNPLMA Round 16 Sub Grant - NV Regional Fuels Reduction Project
LeadImplementerName: North Lake Tahoe Fire Protection District
ProjectDescription: This project has reduced hazardous fuels on lands within the Wildland Urban Interface Defense Zone of Incline Village, NV. 298 acres was treated using hand thinning, and understory burning. It has served to complement near-by fuels reduction projects, and previous treatments where 1st entry hand-thinning has been completed. The project is located near critical water treatment facilities, which are critical for fire-flow in the event of a wildfire, and potential evacuation centers should wildfire be active in the area.

ProjectName: TTD Capital for Operations Enhancements - Short Term
Watershed: Mckinney Creek, General Creek, Meeks Creek, Sierra Creek, Lonely Gulch Creek, Paradise Flat, Rubicon Creek, Bliss State Park, Edgewood Creek, Bijou Park, Eagle Creek, Cascade Creek, Bijou Creek, Tallac Creek, Upper Truckee River, Trout Creek, Camp Richardson, Taylor Creek, Lake Tahoe Waterbody
ProjectDescription: This project includes fleet and facilities for Emerald Bay and Echo Pass Services including  five additional diesel-electric hybrid trolleys needed to operate the service at the envisioned frequency. This project will make improvements to Emerald Bay's eastern parking area to include a bus boarding and alighting area separate from street and parking lot traffic.  The project will also create a safe environment for the bus to make a left turn from the terminal to return to South Lake Tahoe. This project will also construct enhanced bus stops at Echo Summit, Adventure Mountain, Mt. Ralston, Sierra at Tahoe, Camp Sacramento, and Strawberry.

ProjectName: Glenbrook Fuels Reduction Project
ProjectDescription: The Glenbrook Fuels Reduction Project is a forest fuels reduction project that will create a shaded fuel break on between 161 and 200 acres of overstocked forest within the defense zone of the wildland urban interface in the region.   The proposed project is designed to modify fire behavior and reduce flame lengths to 4 feet during 90th percentile fire weather.  This type of forest thinning project will enable firefighters to engage in structure protection in the event of a wildland fire.

ProjectName: Diamond Peak Lodge Fuels Reduction Project
LeadImplementerName: North Lake Tahoe Fire Protection District
ProjectDescription: The Diamond Peak Lodge Fuels Reduction Project reduces hazardous wildland fuels on 63 acres of local government owner land in the wildland-urban interface of Incline Village, NV to mitigate wildfire risk to the community and improve forest health. There are 500 condominium units near-by. The project removed ladder fuels, reduced dead and downed debris, increased crown to base height, reduced brush height and continuity and thinning trees from below to reduce potential fire intensity and protect nearby resources from catastrophic wildfire.

ProjectName: Upper Diamond Peak Fuels Reduction Project
LeadImplementerName: North Lake Tahoe Fire Protection District
ProjectDescription: The Diamond Peak Planning Area is within the Defense and Threat Zones of the Wildland-Urban Interface of Incline Village, Nevada. Adjacent high density residential developments include Tyrolian Village and Bitterbrush Condominiums. A fire in the area could restrict the limited evacuation routes for the 500 nearby residences. Fuel reduction treatments provide a safer working environment for firefighters, protect public evacuation routes, and introduce tactical opportunities to redirect a fire approaching from the south. There are 130.5 treatable acres within the larger project area. Smaller projects will serve to treat these acres over time and as funding can be secured.

ProjectDescription: Successful implementation of the Tahoe yellow cress (TYC) Conservation Strategy (CS2015) will continue to prevent the need to list TYC under the ESA and will protect the species per California and Nevada State law. ProjectName: Marlette Creek Restoration and SR28 Crossing Improvement Project
ProjectDescription:
This project near Thunderbird lodge on Lake Tahoe's east shore proposes to restore a portion of Marlette Creek to improve stream function, water quality, and fish habitat and provide erosion control and stormwater treatment at directly connected outfalls from SR 28. 
Specifically (1) Capture and treat State Route 28 stormwater runoff prior to entering Marlette Creek by installing treatment at each stormwater outfall.(2) Repair incision and stabilize the bed of S. Fork of Marlette Creek and provide fish passage. (3) Provide fish passage at the SR 28 culvert. ProjectDescription: Target invasive fish species are contributing to declines in native and recreational non-native fish, alterations in food-web dynamics, and reductions in water quality. An IS/ND and IEC/FONSE was completed for the Target Invasive Fish Control Program at Lake Tahoe to authorize a selection of mechanical fish control methods that can be implemented in locations of suitable habitat for the target species over the next 20 years. LeadImplementerName: U.S. Forest Service - Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit
ProjectDescription: The Meeks Bay restoration project involves the planning for the future of the marina, and restoration of the Meeks Creek lagoon. The shallow warm waters of the marina create a breeding ground for Aquatic Invasive Species. The desired condition is to restore the lagoon to a natural condition while providing a recreation experience which is lighter on the landscape. In addition, the project includes upgrades to current camping and day use recreation facilities and opportunities. Phase 1 (planning & design) est. $2 million; Phase 2 (implementation and Hwy 89 bridge replacement) est. $11 million.

ProjectName: Lakeside Beach and Lakeside Marina Aquatic Invasive Plant Control UV Light Pilot
ProjectDescription: This project tested UV-C light technology in two lake environments, an enclosed waterbody (marina) and an open water body (beach littoral) system, for the treatment of aquatic invasive plant infestations. The technology has previously shown success in laboratory testing where results indicated complete mortality of plants and plant fragments treated with UVC light. In this study, a decrease in plant percent cover, mean plant height, and thus plant density, was observed. The results of this study demonstrated the efficacy of this method as a useful tool for controlling aquatic invasive plants and provided information to support future environmental document analysis and permitting needs.

ProjectName: Polaris Creek and Wetland Restoration, Phase I Planning
ProjectDescription: The creek and wetland complex found along Polaris Creek has been significantly impaired due to development of residential and recreational facilities. The degraded wet meadow habitat areas adversely impact the associated fish and wildlife habitat values, and these disturbances have significant impacts on water quality, floodplain processes, and fish passage. In Phase I, an Opportunities and Constraints Feasibility Analysis has been conducted to explore the restoration potential of the Polaris Creek and Wetland complex while also addressing and accommodating recreational uses that currently occur at this site; a ball field, playground, campground, and restroom/parking facilities.

ProjectName: Sand Harbor Aquatic Invasive Asian Clam Control
ProjectDescription: A population of Asian clams was discovered in Sand Harbor in 2015.  Surveyors estimated the population size at approximately 1.5 acres in the boat landing area of Sand Harbor- Lake Tahoe Nevada State Park.  Prior to work commencing, the population was estimated at 6 acres.  Once treatment began in 2017, divers discovered clams in additional areas.  The infestation was estimated to be over 25 acres in extent. With the larger infestation, the approach focused on maintenance rather than localized eradication. Three rounds of barrier relocation occured that treated a total of approximately 9.3 acres. Barriers were removed in June of 2020. See projet images for post-project results.

ProjectName: North Shore Sugar Pine Restoration for Mountain Pine Beetle Outbreak Recovery
LeadImplementerName: UC Davis Tahoe Environmental Research Center
ProjectDescription: Our project will collect seedlings from 100 local and diverse sugar pine trees from Crystal Bay to Tahoe City for reforestation and mountain pine beetle outbreak recovery. Five years of drought has resulted in significant mountain pine beetle-mediated mortality in sugar pine trees on the north shore of Lake Tahoe. We will collect and cultivate sugar pine seed and seedlings in 2017-2018 so that in 2020 2-year old seedlings can be out-planted at north shore restoration sites at Tahoe Vista (USFS, CTC Lands), Carnelian Bay (USFS, CTC Lands), Dollar Hill (CA State Parks and CTC lands), Tahoe City (USFS and CA State Park Lands), and Crystal Bay (NV State Lands and USFS), and private landowner's.

Forest thinning with hand crews on 55 acres will reduce ladder fuels, overcrowded/diseased trees and promote the growth of large resilient residual trees. When a forest is disturbed, surface runoff may increase, generating surface runoff and sediment delivery. In some cases, such disturbance can also release nutrients like phosphorus to runoff and subsurface lateral flow, adversely affecting offsite water quality. If there is no forest management, then the risk of wildfire is increased, as is the probability of elevated erosion rates much greater than those associated with disturbances from forest management.

There was a need for a tool that could predict the impacts of wildfire and compare that to the impacts of fuel management activities. This project was designed to provide such a tool at a sub watershed scale.

Around Lake Tahoe, sections of the Stream Environment Zone, especially those that contain the terminal portions of streams feeding into the lake, are within the Wildland Urban Interface where potential impacts from wildfire are a key concern. A considerable effort has been underway within the LTB to mitigate these potential impacts. An understanding of how wildfire can impact both the WUI and SEZ, along with an assessment of mitigation efforts to date, is therefore critical.

ProjectDescription: Prescribed burning has been conducted in and around the Lake Tahoe Basin (LTB) to maintain natural succession of plant communities and to reduce wildfire danger. During 2011-2012, approximately 2000 acres of wildland in the LTB were subjected to understory or slash-pile burns. Although these prescribed burns are conducted under strict guidelines, they can still be an important source of air pollutants, particularly fine particulate matter (PM2.5), in the LTB. ProjectName: Rosewood Creek Continuation Project
ProjectDescription: The Rosewood Creek Continuation Project seeks to restore an area between two previously completed restorations on Rosewood Creek by constructing in channel grade controls using biostabilization and adding stormwater treatment where it is needed. The project's goals include improving water quality, riparian function, drought resilience, and terrestrial and aquatic habitat. The project completed water quality monitoring on Rosewood Creek that had been ongoing since 2002; the final report was submitted to the Bureau of Reclamation on September 30, 2023.

ProjectName: Angora Creek fish passage improvement
LeadImplementerName: U.S. Forest Service - Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit
ProjectDescription: This project removed a culvert that was a barrier to fish passage and replaced it with a low water crossing that is completely passable to fish. This project, along with culvert retrofits on Angora Creek at View Circle and Lake Tahoe Blvd, make the entire length of Angora Creek accessible to migrating and residential fish.

ProjectName: Angora Creek restoration project - golf course reach
LeadImplementerName: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ProjectDescription: In the mid 1900's Angora Creek was diverted to dry the meadow for grazing. Construction of the Lake Tahoe Golf Course in 1960 on the dry meadow obliterated the eastern third of the meadow and channel. In 1997, the meadow channel was restored by enhancing remnants, constructing new sections of the historic channel and removing dams and drainage ditches. An entirely new channel restored geomorphic function. This two-stage channel was built by excavating a channel and constructing banks with coir fabric encapsulated soil lifts. The project restored geomorphic function, raised the water table and shifted the meadow vegetation to wetter species, improving riparian habitat and water quality.

ProjectName: Angora Creek Restoration Project - Sewer Line Capture
LeadImplementerName: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ProjectDescription: A reach of Angora Creek was captured after sewer construction, taking on a new course following a sewer line that runs down the meadow. This new creek alignment ran in a straight line for over 2,000 feet. This in turn caused severe down-cutting of the creek bed and lowering of the water table, resulting in drying of the meadow vegetation and impaired habitat. The creek was suffering from water quality issues as well because there was effluent from the sewer line leaching into the creek and ground water. State Parks implemented a restoration project in 2002. A new meandering channel was constructed at grade with the meadow, and the sewer line channel was backfilled and re-vegetated.

ProjectName: Blackwood  Creek Fish ladder removal  and Culvert Replacement
LeadImplementerName: U.S. Forest Service - Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit
ProjectDescription: Between  2003 and 2006,  the U.S. Forest Service removed a large concrete fish ladder and replaced a large culvert with a bridge, including reconstruction of adjacent stream channels at both sites. These features were replaced with a series of constructed boulder step pools to maintain a stable stream profile, while restoring function in terms of coarse bed load sediment transport and fish passage. https://www.fs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_DOCUMENTS/fseprd498677.pdf

ProjectName: Blackwood Creek restoration - Phase 1
LeadImplementerName: U.S. Forest Service - Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit

ProjectDescription:
This monitoring program was suspended in 2019 to complete a basin-wide assessment of SEZ condition and will resume in 2020...

TRPA's SEZ monitoring program utilizes the California Rapid Assessment Method (CRAM), which is a wetland monitoring method that measures buffer and surrounding landscape, hydrology, physical structure, and biotic structure to give an overall "score" of function. The program utilizes both a probabilistic and targeted sampling method to assess the overall health of the Tahoe Basin's SEZ. 20 probabilistic "status" sites are visited each year, and 80 permanent "trend" sites are visited every four years. All data is at http://cramwetlands.org

ProjectName: Spooner Landscape Resilience Project
LeadImplementerName: Nevada Tahoe Resource Team – Nevada Division of Forestry
ProjectDescription: The Spooner landscape resilience Project (Spooner LRP) is a 300 acre thinning located east and north of Spooner Lake in Lake Tahoe Nevada State Park. This project focuses on removing trees too large for hand crews.  All felled trees will be removed through a service contract using a helicopter. This project also includes enhancing aspen stands by removing designated conifers. The project is designed to increase forest resilience to disturbance events, particularly drought and wild fire. Tree tops and limbs were chipped and delivered to the American Renewable Power 20MW biomass plant in Loyalton, CA. Logs were trucked to the Sierra Pacific Industries mill in Quincy, CA.

ProjectName: Dollar Creek Forest Health Project
ProjectDescription: The Dollar Creek Forest Health Project restores forest health to improve forest resilience to the impacts of climate change, protect upper watersheds where the state’s water supply originates, promote the long-term storage of carbon in forest trees and soils and minimize the loss of forest carbon from large, intense wildfires, and promotes biodiversity.

ProjectName: Third Creek Restoration
ProjectDescription: This portion of the restoration project fixed eroding stream banks, restored fish habitat, and restored historic floodplain connections to Third Creek between SR 28 and Incline Way.

ProjectName: Lower Rosewood Creek Restoration and Reconfiguration Project
ProjectDescription:
This project moved Rosewood Creek from its alignment that drained directly into Third Creek just downstream of Hwy 28, back to its original alignment which flows into Third Creek just upstream of Lakeshore Blvd. More information on this project can be found in the Third and Incline Creek Watershed Assessment (http://www.ntcd.org/documents/library/3rdandInclineWatershedAssessment.pdf).

The new section of Rosewood Creek has natural processes that prevent erosion and filter out sediment and pollutants before entering Third Creek and the Lake. This project was completed in 2007.

These outreach elements included holding public meetings, direct mailing postcards and brochures, and implementing other shoreline mediation and outreach program elements.

ProjectName: Evaluating the Reintroduction Potential of LCT at Fallen Leaf Lake
ProjectDescription: Research funded by SNPLMA was published in the North American Journal of Fisheries Management titled “Evaluating the Reintroduction Potential of Lahontan cutthroat trout in Fallen Leaf Lake”. Recommendations from this study improved survival and management of LCT and are currently being implemented at Fallen Leaf Lake. These actions include: multiple stocking sites around the lake as a reintroduction strategy; sites with increased habitat complexity; small numbers of fish per site; hydroacoustics use to improve lake trout suppression; and stocking during periods of thermal stratification to minimize encounters with predators.

ProjectDescription: Phase I will focus on informing reintroduction strategies for lacustrine LCT to restore a native fishery of the world’s largest inland cutthroat and assess LCT habitat use. Based on research from the 2012 ecosystem study LCT will be stocked in the southwest area of Lake Tahoe to assess reintroduction strategies and increase recreational fishing opportunities. The study will examine habitat use, distribution and movement patterns by reintroduced LCT, use of nearshore refugia from nonnative lake trout and begin a lake wide, multiple agency assessment of Lake Tahoe tributaries to determine potential spawning areas and mechanisms for minimizing hybridization with nonnative rainbow trout.

ProjectName: Fallen Leaf Recreational Access Project
ProjectDescription: The Fallen Leaf Lake Area represents one of the largest concentrations of recreational use by visitors and residents in the Lake Tahoe Basin.  The proposed path extension will connect to the existing bike trail network from the City of South Lake Tahoe and the Meyers Community. The Project addresses existing safety conditions on Fallen Leaf Road by moving pedestrians and bicyclists from the roadway to a new shared use path extension reducing conflict hazards.  New parking areas near SR 89 and Fallen Leaf Lake Campground will be evaluated to reduce traffic/off roadway parking impacts. The proposed extension is from Fallen Leaf Campground to Tahoe Mountain Road.

ProjectName: Marlette Creek Restoration
LeadImplementerName: U.S. Forest Service - Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit
ProjectDescription: This project complements the NTCD Marlette Creek SR28 Crossing Retrofit and Restoration Project. The South Fork of Marlette Creek is steep and incised with extensive bank erosion. In 2003, the LTBMU removed a man made dam on the S. Fork channel and created a new channel through the former lake bed. This channel eroded and destabilized following completion of that project and requires in-channel stabilization measures and fish habitat improvement.  NEPA, permitting, and construction for restoration and stabilization of this S. Fork channel reach is included in this project.

ProjectName: Saxon Creek Restoration
LeadImplementerName: U.S. Forest Service - Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit
ProjectDescription: Restoration of Saxon Creek targeting the eroding channel, removal of a fish passage barrier, and restoration of three meadows. The watershed above the road is no longer connected to the floodplain due to previous land uses and conifer encroachment. The project includes NEPA and permitting. This restoration project will occur in three phases. Phase 1: Completed 2018. Replacement of aquatic organism passage barrier at Fountain Place Road.  Phase 2: Completed 2022, Adapt. Mgmt 2023. Restore 1,000 feet of channel and floodplain upstream and downstream of the bridge installation area. Phase 3: Channel and meadow restoration in three meadows (60 acres total). Anticipated implementation 2026.

ProjectName: Blackwood Creek Restoration Phase 4
LeadImplementerName: U.S. Forest Service - Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit
ProjectDescription:
Restore approximately 6,000 feet of stream and floodplain by strategic placement of large wood structures and boulders. Four stream reaches are identified for restoration in the Final Lake Tahoe West Restoration Project EA, issued in September 2025.
Impacts were in response to multiple floods occurring over the winter of 2016/17. Two floods exceeded 20-year flood levels. 
Projects are located in untreated areas. Floods caused stream incision, bank erosion and sinuosity loss.

ProjectName: Tahoe Paradise Park Upper Truckee River Stabilization and Restoration Project
LeadImplementerName: U.S. Forest Service - Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit
ProjectDescription: This project will restore the ecological function of the impaired reach of the Upper Truckee River lying between the Washoe Meadows golf course and the Tahoe Pines public access.  In this reach, streambank erosion impacts the UTR and has destroyed sections of established streamside trails on the east bank upstream of and alongside Lake Baron (which is infested with invasive fish and plant species), and on Forest Service land on the west bank. Restoration activities include re-contouring the vertical-cut streambanks & stabilizing by strategic placement of woody debris and boulders, relocation of streamside trails & creation of low-impact public access, and removal of AIS from Lake Baron.

Through public-private partnerships, residents are engaged in stewardship and monitoring, and efficiency is improved by prioritizing and sharing resources across jurisdictions.

ProjectName: Westshore Fire Protection Water Infrastructure Phase 1
ProjectDescription: Madden Creek Water System (MCWS) has only one groundwater source. The Madden interconnection with Tahoe Swiss Village Water System is insufficient due to limited storage and source capacity, which limits the effectiveness.  Interconnection with the McKinney Quail System (MQS) provides sufficient source and storage capacity enhanced fire flows and access to the regional water from the West Lake Tahoe Regional Water Treatment Plant (WLTRWTP).  To provide adequate flow to the MCWS, a water main needs to be upsized in the MQS. In addition, interconnecting Tahoe Cedars Water System with the TCPUD MQS will provide access to a redundant water source, additional storage, and access to the WLTRWTP.

ProjectName: Food Web Interactions Associated with a Lahontan Cutthroat Trout Reintroduction Effort in an Alpine Lake
ProjectDescription: To understand Fallen Leaf Lake food web interactions between nonnative species that prey on or compete with reintroduced LCT a combination of stomach content and stable isotope analyses was used to evaluate trophic characteristics within the aquatic species assemblage. LCT preyed on a variety of prey resources: mysid shrimp, insects, arthropods, signal crayfish and fishes. Diet overlap was greatest between L CT and Mountain Whitefish and both species exhibit a general feeding strategy that allows them to partition prey resources to avoid competitive interactions.  Predation by Lake and Brown Tout on stocked LCT was observed and should be considered in the context of predator management.

ProjectName: Clancy-Pohl Sensitive Land Acquisition
LeadImplementerName: Nevada Tahoe Resource Team – Nevada Division of State Lands
ProjectDescription: The State of NV through the NV Land Bank acquired 7.67 acres of sensitive land in the Granite Springs Subdivision in Lower Kingsbury, Douglas County in 2017. Edgewood Creek flows through the lower portion of the parcel.  The land was verified by TRPA as land capability districts 1b, 1a, 2, 4, and 6 and contains 22,483 square feet of existing/potential land coverage. Existing land coverage/disturbance is being restored using several available funding sources. Land coverage/disturbance restored with TRPA Excess Mitigation Funds has been permanently retired. The NV Land Bank is permanently retiring the parcel from future development and managing the parcel for environmental benefits.

ProjectDescription:
This project tracks fire defensible space inspections (DSIs) performed by multiple partners in the Tahoe Basin beginning in 2017. Prior to 2017, inspections were tracked in this EIP Project: 02.01.01.0050 - Fuels Treatment on Non-Federal Lands.

Defensible space is the cleared area around homes that reduces wildfire intensity.  It  helps homes survive when wind-blown embers land nearby. It helps protect homes and gives firefighters safer access to defend them. 

Defensible space inspections on private parcels are conducted in California by the SLFR, LVFPD, NTFPD, and CALFIRE; and in Nevada TDFPD and NLTFPD.  This project does not track the amount of money spent on DSIs

ProjectDescription: Airport West is a forest fuels reduction project that is located on the City of South Lake Tahoe property along the East side of the Lake Tahoe Airport runway.  The unit will be hand-thinned, piled, then burned.  Project completion is expected in 2017.  6 acres total.

ProjectName: Tahoe Vista Aquatic Invasive Plant Control
ProjectDescription: The aquatic plant removal implemented at Tahoe Vista boat launch is part of a multi-year lake-wide strategy to remove aquatic invasive plants from the nearshore of Lake Tahoe Basin. Eurasian watermilfoil was detected at the boat launch in 2016. Contracted divers installed lake-bottom barriers in 2017 and 2018 to control this infestation. From 2018-2020, divers conducted surveillance monitoring to ensure that a re-infestation of Eurasian watermilfoil does not develop at this site. Funding dependent, this site will be monitored according to the Lake Tahoe Aquatic Plant Monitoring Program (2020).

ProjectName: Tahoma Roads Water Quality Project

ProjectName: Cave Rock Fire Protection Water Infrastructure Phase 1
ProjectDescription: Reconstruction of the Cave Rock Water System to address severely lacking water supply for fire suppression and protection for both municipal and federal lands. The project consists of replacing failing and undersized infrastructure including waterlines, pumping facilities and water storage tanks. Additionally, the improvements will include an intertie to the Douglas County owned Zephyr Water Utility District water system to improve water supply reliability and redundancy. Projected O&M cost saving is reduction in water leak repairs.

ProjectName: D.L. Bliss Fire Protection Water Infrastructure
LeadImplementerName: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ProjectDescription: D. L. Bliss State Park operates an independent water system that supplies the entire park (including residences, visitor center, campground, beaches and fire hydrants) that was constructed in the 1930's and has not been updated.  The water line crosses under Hwy 89 and leaks continuously, reducing the amount of water available for public and firefighting use, and is at high risk of complete failure.  Project includes: new water plant $400k, expanded catch basin $125k, new SCADA system $250k, new well $310k and replacement of two 25,000 gallon redwood tanks with glass-lined steel tanks $225k.  Project also includes full replacement of all water lines, plus new fire hydrants throughout.

ProjectName: Fallen Leaf Lake/Angora Ridge Trail Project
LeadImplementerName: U.S. Forest Service - Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit
ProjectDescription:
The Tahoe Area Mountain Bike Association (TAMBA) and the U.S. Forest Service Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit partnered to build nearly 5 miles of new trail in the Angora Fire burn area connecting neighborhoods to Angora Ridge and Fallen Leaf Lake.  In 2017 TAMBA held over 60 volunteer trail days with about 150 volunteers and 2,000 hours of trail building.  In addition, the new 2 mile Lily Lake Trail connects Lily Lake to Angora Ridge.  This project captures the private funding contribution to the project; the USFS contribution is tracked in "Basin-wide Trail BMP Upgrades and Maintenance 01.01.04.0055 
Project video: http://www.tamba.org/homepage/angora-trail-project-year-end-recap/

ProjectName: Assessment of groundwater nutrients and periphyton biomass in Lake Tahoe
ProjectDescription: Understanding the transformation and fate of nutrients in groundwater and surface waters is of critical importance for protecting and managing water resources in lake systems. In this investigation, we collected nutrient samples from groundwater and surface water during a 9-month monitoring period to evaluate the timing and availability of nutrients in the nearshore zone of Lake Tahoe. We estimated seasonal groundwater discharge using continuous hydraulic head measurements in piezometers placed in the shallow lakebed. The results indicate that groundwater and nutrient discharge through the lakebed appear to stimulate periphyton growth along the eulittoral zone of Lake Tahoe.

ProjectName: Carnelian Bay Fire Protection Water Infrastructure
ProjectDescription: NTPUD owns the Carnelian Bay water system on the north shore of Lake Tahoe which is located at the wildland urban interface in North Tahoe. There are approximately 300 residential and commercial customers in this system.  There was an existing 2,500 linear foot 2-inch diameter watermain that was deficient in fire flows with no fire hydrants. This watermain has been replaced with a new 3,500 linear foot 12-inch watermain with fire hydrants spaced at 500 feet along NLB. The new watermain was extended to the Fulton Water System boundary for a future intertie connection for reliability and redundancy of water supply. This is a high-capacity intertie at 12-inches in diameter.

ProjectName: South Shore Fire Protection Water Infrastructure -Well #1
ProjectDescription: After the Angora Fire, the Lukins Brothers Water Company developed the 2009 Infrastructure Replacement Plan, an 11-phase plan to bring the system up to current standards. Lukins has successfully completed almost 2 phases, funded exclusively by customer contribution, increasing system-wide fire protection by 40%. A new well is the next key step to increase Lukins overall source capacity, which will also will bring a regional benefit through Tahoe Keys Water and STPUD future intertie projects. This project will allow all future upgrades guaranteed water capacity and will decrease the threat of destruction from catastrophic wildfire in a key area of South Lake Tahoe and adjacent USFS lands.

ProjectName: Upper Bijou Park Creek Restoration Project
ProjectDescription: The Upper Bijou Park Creek Restoration Project is a watershed-scale project seeking to address water quality & flooding issues in a phased approach to provide treatment for urban runoff in an approximately 850-acre watershed that discharges to Lake Tahoe via Ski Run Marina. The City completed Phase 1 in 2018 with the Knights Inn redevelopment, replacing the failing storm drain with new treatment basins and conveyance system. The City is currently finishing Phase 2 of the project (design), focused on the large upper watershed that includes 8 separate projects. Phase 3 (construction) begins with one of the projects, Rockwood to Blackwood, in May 2025. The other projects are currently unfunded.

ProjectName: Beowawie Road Slope Repair
ProjectDescription: This project will repair an existing retaining wall along Beowawie Road in Crystal Bay, Nevada. This wall was installed as part of the Crystal Bay Erosion Control Project (1988) and is failing due to extreme runoff during and following the 2017 winter. The failing slope is located within 600 feet of Lake Tahoe, and a complete slope failure would have a negative effect on water quality.

ProjectName: Douglas County Basin Maintenance and Upgrades - Kingsbury Grade/North Benjamin and Donna/Scott Way
ProjectDescription: To complete basin maintenance and upgrades to two Douglas County maintained stormwater basins within the Tahoe basin.  Both basins are located on property owned by the U.S. Forest Service with an easement provided to Douglas County to operate these basins.  The basins proposed for maintenance are located at Donna Way and Scott Drive (APN 1319-18-301-001) and Kingsbury Grade and North Benjamin Drive (APN 1319-19-202-002). Due to sediment accumulation and vegetation growth the basins no longer hold their original design volume of stormwater.  This project will remove the accumulated sediment and vegetation, restore original basin geometry, and construct a hard articulated block basin bottom.

ProjectName: Rubicon Trail Accessibility Improvements
LeadImplementerName: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ProjectDescription: This project involves accessibility improvements to a portion of the existing Rubicon Trail at D.L. Bliss State Park.  Accessibility improvements are in compliance with California State Parks accessibility guidelines and associated legal mandates.  The project will create approximately 1 mile of accessible trail by reconstructing portions of the existing trail surface with minor reroutes and/or the addition of rock retaining walls, benches, parking, and directional signage.

ProjectDescription: This project proposes to develop a comprehensive environmental planning document to restore ecological and hydrological characteristics of meadows on National Forest System lands in the Lake Tahoe Basin.  We have already completed a very similar NEPA document which focused on six meadows. We are currently restoring these meadows.  These past experiences of writing the NEPA document and evaluating the feasibility of different restoration techniques are very advantageous for moving forward with a stream-lined, broader-scale document. As a result, we anticipate this planning project would take fewer than two years to complete.

ProjectName: Incline Flume Trail Reconstruction
LeadImplementerName: U.S. Forest Service - Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit
ProjectDescription: The “Incline Flume” trail is located above Incline Village and is primarily accessed from Mt Rose Highway (HWY 431). It connects to numerous other trails and access points, such as the Tyrolean trail, Diamond Peak access roads and Tunnel Creek trail/road in Lake Tahoe Nevada State Park on the south end. This project provided trail maintenance and major reconstruction of several failed segments. It is popular with trail runners, mountain bikers, walkers and hikers - of all ability levels. This project has been a collaborative effort with Friends of Incline Trails, the USFS, the Tahoe Fund, and many local volunteers.

ProjectName: North Benjamin Parking Lot Recreation and Water Quality Improvements
LeadImplementerName: U.S. Forest Service - Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit
ProjectDescription: This project improved the informal parking at Kingsbury Trailhead. Parking was occurring on native surface, and was expanding into surrounding vegetation as the trailhead grew in popularity. Parking lot improvements include: paving and striping, BMPs, a vehicle turnaround and OHV loading ramp, restrooms, and relocating the existing kiosk.

ProjectDescription: The 2012-2015 drought was an exceptional period of warm and dry weather that impacted water and ecological resources in the Lake Tahoe Basin (LTB). Although above average temperature and below average precipitation occurred in all four years, the patterns varied across years and in different parts of the LTB. Water year (WY) 2012 and 2015 were the most exceptional in terms of below average precipitation (30 and 36% below the long term average, respectively). In general the southern end and higher elevations of the LTB experienced the warmest drought.  Overall Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI) was less severe than during 1987-1990 drought.

ProjectDescription: The purpose of the Scenic Quality Improvement Program (SQIP) is twofold: to establish scenic management standards and criteria, and to develop site specific measures for each scenic unit (roadway and shoreline) not in attainment of the adopted scenic thresholds.  The original program was adopted by the TRPA Governing Board in 1989 and has not been updated since then. The update will assess the scenic units not in attainment and outline specific measures to improve scenic quality in those units which will be implemented through project review.

ProjectName: North Upper Truckee SEZ Restoration Project
ProjectDescription: This Project is part of the North Upper Truckee Erosion Control Project series (I & II completed in the 1990s) with the main focus on enhancement of the stream environment zone (SEZ) area along North Upper Truckee Road.  The main goal of the project is to enhance the SEZ area along North Upper Truckee Road from Grizzly Mountain Drive to Lake Tahoe Blvd.

Scenic deterioration results from types of development that dominate or are incompatible with the natural landscape, are in locations visible from major roadways, block important views and remove vegetation and natural features, and alter the topography. The scenic resource evaluation assesses changes in scenic conditions relative to TRPA threshold standards.

ProjectName: Kingsbury General Improvement District (KGID) Street Sweeper
ProjectDescription: KGID maintains 22 miles of roadway within the Lake Tahoe Basin. The purchase of a new high efficiency street sweeper will enhance KGID’s ability to maintain its roadway system, which will ultimately help Douglas County reduce the flow of fine sediment to the lake and meet its required TMDL mandate.  The County has registered KGID's road network within the Stormwater Tools and will receive TMDL credit for road operations, as long as the road score is at 3.0 or above.  KGID will enter into a contract with Douglas County to sweep the roads according to an approved sweeping schedule.  See https://stormwater.laketahoeinfo.org/RoadRegistration/Detail/3 for more information.

ProjectName: Aquatic Invasive Species Veliger Monitoring
Jurisdiction: City of South Lake Tahoe, Douglas County, NV, El Dorado County, CA, Placer County, CA, Washoe County, NV, Tahoe Regional Planning Agency, U.S. Forest Service - Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit, Carson City County, NV
ProjectDescription:
The Tahoe Regional Planning Agency monitors for the presence of aquatic invasive species. Monthly plankton tows are conducted in Lake Tahoe from May through September. The purpose is to detect quagga and zebra mussel and Asian clam veligers. After the plankton tow is taken, the sample is sent to a lab to detect the presence of larval stage invasive species.  

The invasive golden mussel was detected in the Bay/Delta of California in the later part of 2024. This monitoring will also be used for this new species to North America as well.

The collective results of this effort would be used to produce status reports, and design projects focused on supporting resilience of the Lake Tahoe Basin landscape under a changing climate.  The disciplines include plants, fungi, fish, amphibians, reptiles, mammals, birds, and associated habitats. Species evaluated would include, but not limited to, ESA-listed, Forest Service Sensitive, and TRPA Special Interest species.

With the help of peer agencies, the CAAP will identify gaps and opportunities in their climate adaptation work. Participants will subsequently identify specific actions that they themselves commit to implementing. The CAAP will provide key information that will be utilized in planning efforts for future project implementation.

ProjectDescription: This effort built upon previous AIS plans to guide AIS funding, planning, implementation, monitoring, and assessment of AIS control efforts in the Basin. Through a collaborative approach with key agencies, scientists, and stakeholders, the strategy identifies relevant AIS metrics consistent with EIP objectives, sets clear short and long-term management targets, and developed a plan to achieve short-term targets. The plan also includes a funding strategy to leverage federal, state, local, and private contributions necessary to achieve the targets. This plan developed metrics and targets to guide strategic AIS control efforts in the Basin.

ProjectName: Emerald Bay State Park Aquatic Invasive Plant Surveillance and Response
LeadImplementerName: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ProjectDescription:
Annual monitoring is performed by contract scuba divers and the CA State Parks Dive Team to detect and remove any invasive aquatic weeds in Emerald Bay. Emerald Bay was infested with Eurasian watermilfoil and curly-leaf pondweed starting in 2007 and after implementing a removal project that was completed in 2015, this monitoring program was designed and implemented to continue the effort to keep invasive species from establishing in the bay. There is no completion date for this project. It will continue indefinitely. 

See project 01.03.01.0041 - Emerald Bay Aquatic Invasive Plant Control for most recent information.

ProjectDescription: This is a three-year study on the effects of white satin moth infestations on bird communities at Lake Tahoe. This invasive moth species has caused significant aspen defoliation and mortality in Lake Tahoe Nevada State Park since the early 2010s, and this project will be the first to document impacts to bird communities that rely on aspen habitats at Lake Tahoe. Point-count bird surveys and nest monitoring will be conducted during the breeding season, and aspen habitat assessments will be conducted each year in order to quantify whether major structural changes in aspen communities caused by white satin moths have any effects on bird abundance, diversity, and nesting success.

ProjectName: Emerald Bay SP UC Davis Osprey Spatial Data Analysis
LeadImplementerName: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ProjectDescription:
The osprey is a special status indicator species for the TRPA's environmental threshold evaluation. In order to better understand the relationship between osprey breeding success and human disturbance, Parks teamed up with UNR to conduct a spatial and statistical analysis 
from almost thirty years of osprey nesting data in Emerald Bay and D.L. Bliss State Parks.  Emerald Bay comprises of the most concentrated area of active nests around Lake Tahoe and is also one of the most highly visited recreation areas on the lake. Statistical analysis was developed for reproductive success in relation to distance from potential disturbance factors such as roads, trails, and campground facilities.

ProjectName: Forestry - Meadowvale SRA Grant
ProjectDescription: This 10-acre fuel hazard reduction project was designed to protect the south end of Country Club Estates from ignitions originating on U.S. Highway 50.

ProjectDescription: This project tested and evaluated methods that could be used to estimate the distribution and biomass of metaphyton in the nearshore and washing up off of three beaches where metaphyton had been observed in the past: Round Hill Pines Beach in NV and El Dorado and Regan Beaches in CA. Observations through time for Lake Tahoe suggest metaphyton is heaviest in mid-summer to early fall. Monitoring was conducted during two occasions between July and September 2015, as it was believed this would capture the period of peak metaphyton abundance. One transect extending perpendicular to the shore was established at each of the study sites. Monitoring included biomass sampling and photo documentation.

ProjectName: Evaluation of Biochar Amendments for Nutrient and Fine Sediment Retention in Stormwater Treatment Applications
